title: How to make a pivot table in Excel on Mac: steps for Microsoft 365 users
metaTitle: How to Make a Pivot Table in Excel on Mac (Step by Step)
description: How to make a pivot table in Excel on Mac: click a cell, choose Insert > PivotTable, tick your fields, then refresh when your data changes.
targetKeyword: how to make a pivot table in excel on mac
intro: To make a pivot table in Excel on a Mac, click any cell in your data, choose Insert > PivotTable, pick New Worksheet, and click OK. Excel then adds a blank pivot table, and you tick the fields in the PivotTable Fields list to fill it in.
tldr: Click one cell in your data, then choose Insert > PivotTable.
Pick New Worksheet, click OK, and tick fields in the PivotTable Fields list.
Right-click a value and choose Field Settings to switch Sum to Count or Average.
After the data changes, right-click the pivot table and choose Refresh, or press ⌥ F5.

blocks.text: What a pivot table does

A pivot table groups rows that share a value, then adds up or counts the numbers in each group. It does not change your source data. It builds a summary on top of the data, so you can ask new questions without rewriting formulas.

Say you have a sheet of orders with a region, a product and a sales amount. Put Region in Rows and Sales in Values, and you get total sales for each region. Add Product to Columns, and the same summary becomes a grid of region by product.
Choose your layout before you click anything

blocks.caption: Common layouts and where each field goes

blocks.text: Decide the question before you open the dialog. Name the field that goes down the side, the field that goes across the top, and the number you want to total. That order saves a lot of dragging around later.
Clean up your data before you insert the PivotTable

Most pivot table problems start in the source data, not in Excel. The PivotTable reads the range you give it. A blank row in the middle of that range can cut it short, so rows below the gap never show up in the summary.

Give every column a header in row 1. Short names such as Date, Region, Product and Sales work well. Excel uses those headers as field names. A blank header causes an error message, covered in the troubleshooting list below.

items: Keep one header row, with a name in every column.
Delete blank rows and blank columns inside the data.
Store dates as real dates, not as text that only looks like a date.
Make sure numbers are numbers. Text in a Sales column is counted, not summed.

blocks.text: Converting the range to a table helps most. Choose Insert > Table, and the table grows when you add rows underneath it. Point the pivot table at that table, and new rows arrive after a refresh.
PivotTable or Recommended PivotTable on Mac

Excel for Mac has two ways in. Insert > PivotTable gives you a blank pivot table and full control over every field. Insert > Recommended PivotTable asks Excel to analyze the data, shows several layout options, and creates the one you pick on a new sheet when you click OK.

Recommended PivotTables are for Microsoft 365 subscribers only. They belong to the connected experience, so if you opt out of that experience, you cannot use them. An older Microsoft article lists the feature only under Windows, so check your own Insert menu before you look for it.
Add fields and change the layout
The PivotTable Fields list has field names at the top and four boxes at the bottom: Filters, Columns, Rows and Values. Tick a field and Excel places it. Drag it into another box to change the layout.

Text fields usually go to Rows or Columns, because they label groups. Numbers belong in Values, because Excel totals them. A date can go to Rows as well. Right-click a date value and look for Group if you want months or years instead of single days.
Filters sit above the table. Use one to look at a single region without changing the rows. A filter only hides values inside the pivot table. Your source data stays the same.
How to change Sum to Count or Average on Mac

Excel sums numbers by default. If you want the number of orders instead of total sales, change the calculation. On Mac, the command is called Field Settings. Windows calls the same command Value Field Settings.

Count works on text and numbers, so it is the right choice for counting orders or customers. Average, Max and Min work on numbers. If a value looks odd, check the source column for text and blank cells first.
Changing the calculation never alters your source data. It only changes how the pivot table summarizes the rows in that field.
How to refresh a pivot table on Mac after your data changes
A pivot table does not update on its own. Add a row to the source data, and the summary stays the same until you refresh. This catches a lot of people off guard, so build the habit early.

Right-click a cell in the pivot table and choose Refresh. To update every pivot table in the workbook, use PivotTable Analyze > Refresh > Refresh All. A Microsoft Q&A thread warns that Refresh All updates every PivotTable in the workbook, so check the others first.

The keyboard route is ⌥ F5. A Microsoft Q&A moderator confirmed it after testing. Some Mac setups need fn with ⌥ F5, depending on System Settings. Shortcuts can also be reassigned in Tools > Customize Keyboard.
A vendor's guide ran the refresh steps on Excel 16.114.1 on macOS 26.5. That is one vendor's test, so treat the version as a sample, not a promise.
Automatic refresh and newer pivot table features

PivotTable Auto Refresh is an Insider feature for Excel for Mac. Microsoft says it needs Mac version 16.99 or later, and it is available to Beta Channel users. Turn it on by selecting the pivot table, then choosing PivotTable Analyze > Auto Refresh.
Microsoft's October 2025 update added a spill error to PivotTables, the same dynamic array error you see in ordinary formulas. Microsoft made it available to Insider users on Windows and Mac.
Insider features change often. If the menu item is missing, your copy is probably not on the Beta Channel. The regular steps in this guide still work without it.
Build a pivot table from data outside the workbook

You can build a pivot table from an external source, such as a database. Go to Data > New Database Query. For a SQL database, choose SQL Server ODBC. For another source, choose From Database, add the data source, and click OK.
Preview the result with Run, then click Return Data. In the Import Data dialog, choose PivotTable. The PivotTable Builder opens next, so you can add, remove or move fields.
A non-SQL source needs an ODBC driver installed on your Mac. If the source does not appear, install the driver and try again.
What Excel for Mac does not include

Power Pivot is not supported in Excel for Mac, according to a volunteer moderator's answer in Microsoft's Q&A forum. That thread gives no Excel version. If your model depends on Power Pivot, build it on Windows or use a different tool.
The Data Model options, such as Add this data to the Data Model, appear only in the Windows section of Microsoft's get-started article. On Mac, plan on one flat table for each pivot table.
Shortcut differences also catch people. A vendor's test found that the Windows shortcut Alt, N, V did not work on Mac. Use Insert > PivotTable from the menu instead.
Mistakes people make with pivot tables on Mac
The first mistake is a range that stops early. Check the range in the Create PivotTable dialog before you click OK. If it ends at a row you did not expect, cancel and clean up the source.
The second is a field in the wrong box. A field in Columns when you wanted Rows changes the whole grid, and the totals look wrong. Look at the Rows and Columns boxes first, then at the Values box.
The third is forgetting to refresh. If a total stays the same after you added data, refresh before you check your formulas. Most of the time the numbers were right, and the summary was old.
What to do next with your pivot table
Once the first pivot table works, change one thing at a time. Add a second field to Columns, then a filter, then a different calculation. Each change shows you how the grid responds.

If you work with data every day, the job pages show pivot table steps alongside typical data for each role. The [data analysts page](/for/data-analysts/excel) covers cleaning and Power Query. The [Excel page](/apps/excel) explains what voice help looks like inside Excel for Mac.

faq.question: Where is the PivotTable button in Excel for Mac?
faq.answer: It sits on the Insert tab of the ribbon. Click a cell in your data first, then choose Insert > PivotTable. If you click an empty cell, Excel may not find the range you meant.

faq.question: Why does my pivot table not update when I change the data?
faq.answer: Pivot tables only change when you refresh them. Right-click inside the table and choose Refresh, or press ⌥ F5. If new rows still do not appear, point the pivot table at a table made with Insert > Table.

faq.question: Why are my numbers counted instead of summed?
faq.answer: Excel switches to Count when a column holds text. Look for text that looks like a number, convert it to a real number, then refresh. Change the calculation back to Sum with Field Settings.

faq.question: What is the difference between PivotTable and Recommended PivotTable?
faq.answer: Insert > PivotTable gives you a blank table and full control. Insert > Recommended PivotTable has Excel analyze the data and offer several layouts, then creates the one you pick on a new sheet. Recommended PivotTables need a Microsoft 365 subscription.

faq.question: Can I put the pivot table on the same sheet as my data?
faq.answer: Yes. In the Create PivotTable dialog, choose Existing Worksheet, then click the cell where the table should start. Leave empty space below or to the right, because the table grows as you add fields.

faq.question: Does Power Pivot work in Excel for Mac?
faq.answer: No. A volunteer moderator's answer in Microsoft's Q&A forum says Power Pivot is not supported in Excel for Mac. If you need it, build that part of the workbook on Windows.

steps.name: Clean up the source data
steps.text: Put one header in row 1 for every column, such as Date, Region, Product and Sales. Delete blank rows and blank columns inside the range. Excel reads the whole block, and a blank row can cut the range short.
steps.tip: Choose Insert > Table to turn the range into a table. A table grows when you add rows, so the pivot table can pick them up on refresh.

steps.name: Click one cell in the data
steps.text: Click any single cell inside the range or table. Excel usually detects the full range from that cell, so you do not need to select every column.

steps.name: Open the PivotTable command
steps.text: Click the Insert tab on the ribbon, then click PivotTable. The Create PivotTable dialog opens and fills in the range or table name for you.
steps.tip: Recommended PivotTable can appear in the same Insert menu. Microsoft's current article lists it for Mac, but your menu may differ by version.

steps.name: Check the range and pick a location
steps.text: Confirm the range or table name in the dialog. Choose New Worksheet to keep the pivot table apart from your data. Or choose Existing Worksheet, then click the cell where the table should start.

steps.name: Click OK
steps.text: Click OK. Excel adds a blank PivotTable and opens the PivotTable Fields list. A blank grid is normal at this point, because nothing is summarized yet.

steps.name: Tick the fields you want
steps.text: In the PivotTable Fields list, tick each field you want to use. Excel usually places text fields in Rows and numbers in Values. Drag any field into the Filters, Columns, Rows or Values box to change the layout.
steps.tip: If a number lands in Rows, drag it into Values. Numbers in Rows give you one line per value, which is rarely what you want.

steps.name: Change how values are summarized
steps.text: Click the field in the Values box, or right-click a value in the table. Choose Field Settings, then pick Sum, Count, Average, Max or Min.
steps.tip: Mac calls this command Field Settings. Windows calls it Value Field Settings, so Windows guides may use a different name.

steps.name: Refresh after the data changes
steps.text: Right-click inside the pivot table and choose Refresh. To update every pivot table in the workbook, use PivotTable Analyze > Refresh > Refresh All.
steps.tip: Refresh All updates every pivot table in the workbook, so check the other sheets before you run it.

shortcuts.action: Open a filter or PivotTable field pop-up menu

troubleshooting.problem: "The PivotTable field name is not valid"
troubleshooting.fix: One column has no header in row 1. Give every column a name, then try Insert > PivotTable again.

troubleshooting.problem: New rows do not show up
troubleshooting.fix: Right-click the pivot table and choose Refresh, or press ⌥ F5. If rows still go missing, turn the data into a table with Insert > Table and point the pivot table at that table.

troubleshooting.problem: Numbers are counted instead of summed
troubleshooting.fix: Text cells in the column make Excel choose Count. Convert the text to real numbers, refresh, then check Field Settings and pick Sum.

troubleshooting.problem: Refresh All changed a pivot table I did not expect
troubleshooting.fix: Refresh All updates every pivot table in the workbook. Check the other sheets before you use it, or refresh only the table you are working on.
Try fn with ⌥ F5, since some System Settings need it. If that fails, check the shortcut in Tools > Customize Keyboard, because shortcuts can be reassigned.

troubleshooting.problem: Power Pivot or Data Model options are missing
troubleshooting.fix: Excel for Mac does not support Power Pivot, and the Data Model options appear only in Microsoft's Windows steps. Build the model on Windows or simplify the data to one table.
